doc.title: JJ Johnson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: First paid work and the dance-band repertoire
summary: Playing dances with LaVon Kemp and Clarence Love, Glenn Miller and Lunceford arrangements, and talk of Erskine Hawkins.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: After you graduated from high school, was that when you had your first professional engagement, or were you working professionally while you were still in high school?

My best recollection is [that] there were a few bucks to be earned playing with bands like LaVon Kemp and Clarence Love, who was kind of active in this area. I played with him on occasion. But I don’t have a clear recollection of compensation on a professional level until after graduating high school and leaving Indianapolis. I can’t be very accurate about playing for money, shall we say, here in Indianapolis. And yet I do recall – I have a vague recollection – yes, there were some situations where we were paid for playing at a dance, for example, or playing a social function, for example, or what not.
In terms of the kind of music that you would be playing with a band like LaVon Kemp, let's say you were playing for a dance. What kinds of pieces would people expect to hear you play at that time?
Obviously dance music. A lot of it was music that was prevalent by big name white bands, shall we say. For example, let's take Glenn Miller’s [Johnson sings the opening measures of In the Mood].
In the Mood?

In the Mood, String of Pearls, and things like that. LaVon Kemp and bands similar to LaVon Kemp’s would have arrangements of these very well-known and very popular tunes of the day as played by other more prominent big white bands.
Would these . . .
Plus some things by people like Sy Oliver or Lunceford and the other – it was a mixture of things, a mixture as far as repertoire.
Uh huh.
The piece I was trying to think of with the band was Southern Fried.
Ah, there you go. Things like that. Yeah. Tuxedo Junction. What was the name of that band? Tuxedo Junction.
That was the . . .
They were big in this area.
Erskine Hawkins.
Erskine Hawkins. He got big outside of this area.
Fact is, I saw him in the Catskills. He died earlier this year.
Oh, really? Was he still active up until his death?
He had a quintet up in the Catskills.
He played trumpet.
Yeah. "The Gabriel of the Trumpet."
"The Gabriel of the Trumpet." Isn’t that remarkable.
